See also: Triangle

English

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]
PIE word
*tréyes

From Middle English triangle, from Old French triangle, from Latin triangulum, noun use of adjective triangulus (“three-cornered, having three angles”), from trēs (“three”) + angulus (“corner, angle”), equivalent to tri- +‎ -angle.

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • (UK) IPA(key): /ˈtɹaɪəŋɡəl/, /ˈtɹaɪˌæŋɡəl/
  • (US) enPR: trī'-ăng-gəl, IPA(key): /ˈtɹaɪˌæŋɡəl/
  • Audio (US):(file)
  • Rhymes: -aɪæŋɡəl
  • Hyphenation: tri‧an‧gle
  • Rhymes: -æŋɡəl

Noun

[edit]

triangle (plural triangles)

  2. (geometry) A polygon with three sides and three angles.
    • 1981, William Irwin Thompson, The Time Falling Bodies Take to Light: Mythology, Sexuality and the Origins of Culture, London: Rider/Hutchinson & Co., page 22:
      The wedge-shaped character was the triangle, the archaic Paleolithic sign of the vulva; the pubic triangle was at the end of the phallic stylus.
  3. (US, Canada) A set square.
  4. (music) A percussion instrument made by forming a metal rod into a triangular shape which is open at one angle. It is suspended from a string and hit with a metal bar to make a resonant sound.
  5. (billiards) A triangular piece of equipment used for gathering the balls into the formation required by the game being played.
  6. A love triangle.
    • 2009, Neil McDonald, Quadrant, November 2009, No. 461 (Volume LIII, Number 11), Quadrant Magazine Limited, page 104:
      One of the writers' most pleasing inventions was to treat the triangle love story as comedy.
  7. (systemics) The structure of systems composed with three interrelated objects.
  8. A draughtsman's square in the form of a right-angled triangle.
  9. (historical, usually in the plural) A frame formed of three poles stuck in the ground and united at the top, to which people were bound for corporal punishment.
    • 1851, Henry Mayhew, London Labour and the London Poor, published 1861:
      I was flogged in 1840. To this day I feel a pain in the chest from the triangles.
    • 1868, “The Week”, in The Nation‎[1], volume 6, number 149:
      But nothing is said as to what we are to do with the negro when we have cut him off from absolute dominion; we are not informed if we may spread him on the triangles as aforetime;
  10. Any of various large papilionid butterflies of the genus Graphium.
    Synonym: bluebottle
  11. (rail transport) A triangular formation of railway tracks, with a curve on at least one side.
    • 1961 March, ""Balmore"", “Driving and firing modern French steam locomotives”, in Trains Illustrated, page 147:
      After turning on the triangle at Jeumont, we set off light engine back to Aulnoye.
    Synonym: wye

Synonyms

[edit]
  • (polygon): threeside, trigon (rare)
  • (love triangle): love triangle, menage à trois
  • See also Thesaurus:triangle
  • See also △ (symbol)
